tldr: This paper presents UniWAM, which integrates a VLM for high-level language reasoning, a video generation model for predicting physical world dynamics, and an action predictor for precise control into a single MoT architecture. Combining pre-training on multi-source human and robot data with custom post-training techniques, it achieves strong generalization to unseen environments and executes long-horizon tasks on real robots.
hero_caption: Overview of UniWAM. Taking multi-source pre-training data on the left (VQA, human egocentric video, and real-world robot demonstrations) as input, the central Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture jointly learns physical reasoning, world generation, and action prediction. As shown in the radar chart at the top right, it achieves SOTA across simulation (LIBERO, RoboTwin) and real-robot evaluations.
overview:
Recent robot foundation models have heavily focused on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that connect large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) directly to action outputs. However, training on action labels alone tends to provide limited grounding in the dynamics of the physical world. On the other hand, world-action models (WAMs) based on video generation models (VGMs) capture rich spatiotemporal dynamics, yet struggle with semantic reasoning over instructions and understanding under out-of-distribution shifts.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose "UniWAM", a unified model that fuses the semantic reasoning of VLMs with the world dynamics predictive capability of VGMs. Adopting a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture, three experts—a physical reasoner (VLM), a world generator (VGM), and an action predictor—collaborate via a joint attention mechanism.

On the training side, to teach low-level actions without degrading the VLM's inherent language capabilities, the authors introduce "Physical Language" that describes motion differences in natural language. Furthermore, they establish a pre-training recipe that allocates complementary supervision across robot manipulation data, human egocentric video, and VQA data to each component, alongside post-training techniques that initialize flow matching with action history.

Evaluations show superior robustness and generalization over prior methods in simulation environments (LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0). The model also demonstrates high success rates in instruction following and multi-stage tasks on real robots, uncovering a clear log-linear scaling law between dataset scale and validation loss.
contributions: Proposed UniWAM, integrating a VLM-based physical reasoner, a video-generation-based world generator, and a flow-matching action predictor in an MoT architecture.
Introduced "Physical Language" to represent low-level actions in natural language, bridging the domain gap between humans and robots while preserving the VLM's pre-trained knowledge.
Built a pre-training pipeline that optimally allocates complementary supervision across VQA data, ~5,000 hours of human egocentric data, and ~4,363 hours of robot data.
Significantly reduced inference denoising steps while improving control performance via future visual noise augmentation and history-conditioned flow matching initialization.
Empirically uncovered a clear log-linear scaling law with respect to data scale in unified human-robot co-training.

sections.heading: Why combine VLMs with world models?
sections.summary: This section introduces UniWAM to unify the semantic reasoning strengths of VLAs with the physical dynamics strengths of world-action models (WAMs). It presents the overall design to prevent training conflicts across heterogeneous data and adapt the VLM to embodied tasks while retaining its language capabilities.
sections.details:
In recent robotics research, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models built on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved major success. However, relying purely on supervised learning with robot action labels prevents models from fully understanding physical changes in the environment and world dynamics. Conversely, world-action models (WAMs) based on large video generation models (VGMs) acquire physical priors by predicting future frames, yet fall short in complex instruction reasoning and adapting to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments.

To address this, the authors asked whether semantic reasoning and physical prediction could be unified into a single framework, leading to UniWAM. The architecture adopts a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) design, integrating three experts: a physical reasoner, a world generator, and an action predictor.

In pre-training this hybrid model, the paper addresses three major challenges. First, teaching low-level robot actions to a VLM often degrades its pre-trained language abilities. The authors resolve this by introducing "Physical Language", representing low-level actions as natural language text to preserve the VLM's input-output distribution while acquiring action semantics. Second is the optimal allocation of heterogeneous data (VQA, human video, robot trajectories). Complementary supervision is assigned to the appropriate experts: VQA preserves VLM knowledge, human videos teach physical laws, and robot data provides precise action outputs. Third, they developed an automated subtask segmentation and annotation pipeline (EgoANT) for large-scale human videos to ensure data quality.

Furthermore, in post-training, visual noise augmentation on future frames builds robustness against imperfect predictions, and initializing action flow matching with past action history dramatically cuts inference steps while maintaining high performance.

sections.heading: Lineage of VLAs, world-action models, and human video learning
sections.summary: This section reviews three research trends: large-scale robot pre-training, world-action models (WAMs), and learning from human egocentric video. While prior methods only integrated pairs like language-action or video-action, UniWAM stands out by truly unifying semantic reasoning, world generation, and action prediction.
sections.details:
### Large-Scale Pre-training in Robotics
VLA models such as RT-2 and OpenVLA adapt web-scale pre-trained vision-language representations to robot control. More recently, approaches combining flow matching like $\pi_{0}$ and $\pi_{0.5}$, as well as efforts to scale physical grounding using UMI (Unified Manipulation Interface) data (e.g., GEN-0), have emerged. However, these primarily focus on coupling language understanding with action generation, leaving out dense visual dynamics predictions of future states.

### World-Action Models (WAMs)
WAMs built on video generation backbones (such as DreamZero, Motus, and Cosmos Policy) leverage spatiotemporal video priors to predict future pixels or geometric features, enhancing action generation policies. While some methods bypass video generation at inference by utilizing only latent features (e.g., Fast-WAM) or extend into 4D geometry, they still face limitations in high-level language-based reasoning and generalization to unseen instructions.

### Learning from Egocentric Video
Human egocentric data (such as Ego4D and EPIC-KITCHENS) provides a scalable source to complement costly real-robot data. Recent works actively align these with robot action spaces by introducing latent actions or reconstructing human hand trajectories. UniWAM distinguishes itself from prior work by extracting physical insights from these videos and incorporating them directly into pre-training a single architecture that binds language, world prediction, and action together.

sections.heading: How human and robot big data were cleaned and aligned
sections.summary: The authors assembled a dataset combining roughly 4,363 hours of robot manipulation, roughly 5,000 hours of human egocentric video, and VQA data. High-quality training data was achieved via geometric and statistical filtering of robot trajectories and EgoANT, a VLM pipeline for automated segmentation and labeling of human videos.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Data Sources
The pre-training dataset comprises three main streams:
- **Robot Data (~4,363 hours)**: Comprehensively collected single-arm and bimanual manipulation trajectories, including AgiBotWorld2026, Bridge, Droid, Fractal, Robocoin, and Interdata-a1.
- **Human Egocentric Data (~5,000 hours)**: EgoDex with tabletop hand tracking, EgoVerse covering diverse real-world tasks, and VITRA derived from Ego4D and EPIC-KITCHENS.
- **VQA Data**: Diverse question-answering pairs covering spatial reasoning (RoboPoint, etc.), geometric relations (CLEVR, GRiD-3D), and temporal changes or dynamic interactions (RoboVQA, etc.) to maintain the reasoner's pre-trained knowledge.

### 3.2 Data Processing and Cleaning
Because signal quality varies across platforms, strict quality control was enforced.
- **Robot Data Processing**: Non-physical spikes were eliminated using residuals from median filtering and Savitzky-Golay smoothing, and latency compensation was applied via state-action cross-correlation analysis. Forward kinematics (FK) verified the geometric consistency between joint angles and end-effector poses, and coordinate frames were unified with the robot forward direction (+x axis) as the reference.
- **Automated Human Video Segmentation and Annotation (EgoANT)**: To utilize unedited human videos, the authors developed EgoANT, a two-stage VLM pipeline. First, images sampled every 0.5 seconds are compiled into contact sheets to coarsely identify boundaries where object state changes occur (grasping, placing, opening, etc.). Next, the boundary regions are zoomed in to determine precise temporal intervals, and the manipulation content is automatically annotated as concise natural language text formatted as "verb, object, placement destination". Wrist trajectories for both hands are normalized into 14-dimensional pose sequences in the head-camera frame.

sections.heading: UniWAM's core: MoT architecture and hybrid training
sections.summary: UniWAM adopts an MoT architecture integrating Qwen3-VL, the Wan2.2 video generation model, and a flow-matching action predictor. Key highlights include "Physical Language" pre-training that translates actions into text for the VLM, along with fast post-training utilizing future visual noise and action history.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Model Architecture
UniWAM is constructed as a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT). Specifically, it consists of three experts: a "Physical Reasoner" based on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, a "World Generator" based on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, and an "Action Predictor". Each expert contains 30 layers, where tokens interact across layers via a shared Joint Multimodal Attention mechanism. This allows action tokens to be refined while attending simultaneously to high-level semantic context and dynamic future visual predictions.

### 4.2 Pre-training
- **Introduction of Physical Language**: Low-level robot end-effector displacements (translations in cm, rotations in 10-degree increments) are converted into structured text such as "move forward 3 cm, open gripper" and trained using the VLM's autoregressive language modeling loss. This teaches action semantics without compromising the VLM's natural language generation capabilities.
- **Training Losses**: Flow matching losses ($\mathcal{L}_v, \mathcal{L}_a$) are applied to future image latents and action chunks (length 16), while an autoregressive language loss ($\mathcal{L}_u$) is applied to physical language and VQA. The total loss $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_a + w_v \mathcal{L}_v + w_u \mathcal{L}_u$ (with a weight ratio of $1 : 1 : 0.1$) is optimized jointly.

### 4.3 Post-Training
During downstream adaptation, two key techniques are applied:
- **Future Visual Noise Augmentation**: Because generated future images during inference can be noisy, Gaussian noise is injected into future image latents with a 50% probability during training. This forces the action predictor to extract vital control features even from coarse visual representations.
- **History-Conditioned Flow Matching**: Rather than starting action generation from standard Gaussian noise, flow matching begins from a latent representation initialized by adding minor noise ($\eta=0.02$) to the recently executed past action chunk. Providing previous motion continuity as an initial condition allows high-precision action trajectories to be generated in just 2 to 4 denoising steps.

The data comprises human video (~5,072 hours), robot manipulation (~4,959 hours), and VQA (~8.3M samples).

sections.heading: Empirical results: SOTA, resilience to unseen settings, and scaling laws
sections.summary: UniWAM achieved higher success rates than existing models on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, demonstrating particular robustness to environmental perturbations. Real-robot experiments confirmed strong instruction following and long-horizon execution, alongside an empirical log-linear scaling law in human-robot co-training.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Simulation Evaluation
- **In-distribution**: On the LIBERO benchmark, UniWAM achieved an average success rate of 99.2%, outperforming the previous top model (Xiaomi-Robotics-0 at 98.7%). It also attained a 75.14% success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean (C2C).
- **OOD and Robustness**: In LIBERO-Plus across 7 types of perturbations (background, viewpoint, language, lighting, etc.), it recorded the highest overall success rate of 92.6%. On RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Rand (C2R), it achieved 68.32%. The performance drop from C2C to C2R was only 6.82 points, demonstrating remarkable resilience compared to $\pi_{0.5}$ (a 24.70-point drop) and Spatial Forcing (a 50.46-point drop).

### 5.2 Real-Robot Evaluation
Experiments were conducted using an AgileX Piper setup (dual-arm 6-DoF arms with grippers).
- **Instruction-Following Tasks**: Across four tasks (Pick-Anything, Diverse-Interaction, Place-Relative, Drawer-Storage), UniWAM achieved an average task success rate of 67.5% and an instruction-following rate of 82.5%, outperforming $\pi_{0.5}$ by 13.1 points and 21.9 points, respectively.
- **Long-Horizon Tasks**: From a single command to "Tidy up the desk", the robot autonomously completed six sequential milestones including placing cups, operating drawers, and inserting items into pen holders. It reached an average progress score of 5.0 (out of 6), exceeding $\pi_{0.5}$ (4.8) and Motus (3.2).

### 5.3 Scaling Laws and Ablation Studies
In scaling experiments varying robot data (250 to 5,000 hours) and human video ratios, a log-linear relationship between validation loss and dataset scale ($R^2 \approx 0.983$) was observed. The benefit of adding human video becomes prominent once the data volume exceeds 1,000 hours. Furthermore, t-SNE visualizations showed that pre-training with Physical Language causes human and robot latent distributions to overlap cleanly.

Beyond ~1,000 hours of data, the benefit of adding human video (blue curve) clearly outperforms robot-only training (gray curve), exhibiting clear log-linear scaling.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A major step toward general-purpose robots that understand physics
sections.summary: UniWAM is a unified world-action model bringing semantic reasoning, world generation, and action prediction into a single architecture. With rigorous data cleaning, Physical Language, and effective post-training, it achieves superior generalization to unseen environments and efficient inference, demonstrating the scalability of embodied AI.
sections.details:
This work proposed UniWAM, which jointly learns semantic reasoning about the physical world, world modeling, and precise action prediction within a unified framework.

To leverage massive heterogeneous human and robot datasets, the authors established a rigorous data cleaning and automated annotation pipeline (EgoANT). In addition, supervision via Physical Language and a complementary pre-training scheme across components enabled the acquisition of grounded physical knowledge while preserving the VLM's pre-trained language capabilities. During post-training, future visual noise augmentation and history-conditioned flow matching drastically boosted inference speed and robustness.

Through extensive simulation and real-robot experiments, UniWAM demonstrated SOTA performance across in-domain execution, perturbation resilience, OOD generalization, instruction following, and long-horizon tasks. Moreover, revealing a log-linear scaling law in unified human-robot co-training provides valuable guidance for the future development of large-scale robot foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-robot setup and the secret to fewer inference steps
sections.summary: This section covers the setup and task details of the dual-arm robot used in real-world experiments, along with an analysis of inference denoising steps. It highlights how Action-to-Action (A2A) generation initialized with past actions enables precise control in just 2 to 4 denoising steps.
sections.details:
### Real-Robot Tasks and Hardware Setup
The real-robot evaluation setup consists of two AgileX Piper arms (each 6-DoF with parallel grippers) and three cameras (two wrist cameras and one overhead camera). The tabletop is populated with everyday items such as calculators, tissue boxes, drawers, colored markers, clocks, and cups, evaluated across 40 trials per task. For single-arm tasks, the arm closer to the target object is automatically assigned, while bimanual coordination is utilized for cooperative motions such as opening a drawer while inserting an item.

### Efficient Action Generation (A2A vs. N2A)
In the action predictor's denoising process, Noise-to-Action (N2A), which generates actions starting from standard Gaussian noise, was compared against Action-to-Action (A2A), which initializes by adding small noise to the most recent past action chunk. The results confirmed that A2A achieves higher accuracy in just 2 to 4 inference steps than N2A achieves in 10 steps. Consequently, UniWAM adopts 4-step A2A as its default configuration in real-robot deployments, delivering the inference speed necessary for real-time control.

captions.F10: Real-robot experimental setup. Two robot arms, an overhead camera, wrist cameras, and diverse everyday objects (calculators, drawers, clocks, cups, etc.) used in the experiments are shown.

takeaways: Linking a VLM's reasoning power with a video model's dynamics prediction in an MoT structure creates policies highly resilient to perturbations and unseen environments.
Expressing low-level robot actions as natural language (Physical Language) bridges the human-robot domain gap without degrading pre-trained VLM weights.
Human video significantly enhances robot control generalization only at large scales exceeding 1,000 hours, following a clean log-linear scaling law between loss and data volume.
Using past action history as the initial noise state (A2A) reduces flow-matching inference to just 2 to 4 steps while improving control performance.
limitations: Because it is an ultra-large multimodal architecture incorporating a video generation model (Wan2.2 5B), pre-training demands substantial compute, requiring 32 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for 7 days.
At smaller data scales (under 1,000 hours), the domain gap of human egocentric video dominates, leading to observed drops in control performance.
Real-robot evaluations were restricted to tabletop manipulation; verifying its effectiveness on mobile manipulation involving whole-body coordination remains future work.
